chapter: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings
title: 1939 article: his career in outline
summary: The article traces his career from the Gettysburg College summer band and Versatile Five through Harrison-Hollins, Specht, Weems, Goldkette, Voorhees and radio, and his songs with Trumbauer.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: studied piano but started to play the drums without lessons until he found out that there were better drummers than he. Then he studied. When he was in high school, he played with the school band and joined the summer band from Gettysburg College. The band played in Ocean City, New Jersey. When that broke up, Morehouse got a job with a dance orchestra playing the banjo and was good enough to get by. Soon he persuaded the manager to let him send for his drums. Musicians in those days were versatile fellows. Morehouse used to alternate between the drums, the xylophone and a few other instruments. He organized the Versatile Five in which the trumpet player also played the violin and the pianist played the ocharina. When he finished school, he took a job in Pittsburgh with the Harrison-Hollins orchestra. Next he helped Paul Specht form a band which went on a successful trip to England in 1923. He finished his three-year contract with Speck and went with Ted Weems. When the band was reorganized, he joined the Jean Goldkette band. Morehouse's cymbal playing became a byword. When the Goldkette band broke up in 1927, Morehouse went with Don Vorhees's orchestra. It was in 1928 that he started to work on radio. All along, he had been doing recordings. In those days, Morehouse explained, the big band leaders didn't have regular bands. When they got record dates, they called the musicians they wanted. Morehouse was so much in demand, he was kept busy working on records alone.

Name almost any famous band and you will find Morehouse was the drummer on its most popular recordings. After 1928, he stayed on the radio except for brief intervals with Rubinoff and Roger Wolf Kahn. He gave up playing the drums in musical comedies ten years ago. Morehouse says it's a lazy man's job. You learn a score and then play it the same way night after night with your eyes shut, he commented. He played for Rain or Shine and Follow Thru. Morehouse has had to play opera and concert for the radio but his true love is swing. He was the suitcase man with such swing cats as the late Bix Beiderbecke, Miff Moll and Frank Trumbauer. He wrote "Crazy Cat" and "Three Blind Mice" in collaboration with Trumbauer.

Mrs. Morehouse is amused at the $1.98 royalty checks that still come in for those songs which were written 12 years ago. Saxophone solos arranged for the music by Trumbauer are used by most sax students today. Morehouse wrote other songs and confesses the musicians in those days who had record dates would make recordings of their own music and then try the publisher which was much easier than trying to find a publisher first. He hopes to organize a band of his own soon. First, he must reorganize his household. The family is in the throes of moving. Even though it's only down the block. After April 1, the Morehouse address will be 68-31 Ingram Street. He has two children, Suzanne-4 and Jimmy-7. The family moved to Forest Hills from Rego Park five years ago.
